chapter: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
title: Tiger Rag snare blowing and the march medley
summary: He blew against the snare on Tiger Rag; the band had a New Orleans march feel.

bands.name: Conrad Janis and His Tailgate Jazz Band

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: All right. And after you spent some time with Conrad Janis, you went with Wilbur De Paris. You worked with Wilbur De Paris for a couple of years, it seems. While we're on that, apparently on "Tiger Rag," when you started recording "Tiger Rag," you used to blow into the snare drum even back as early as that...
Blow against the snare. So that's what makes that blowing sound on the record.

Now, in this Circle record, there was a medley of the three marches. You had "Bugle Boy" and there's "Gettysburg" and "1919." These marches were done in the old march spirit. But the others were rather Modern Dixieland, sort of. Was this a style that you enjoyed playing?

Yes. That band sounded more like a New Orleans band. It sounded more like a New Orleans band, to get... Especially the way the trumpet player and the clarinet player, he... He had a style of his own, Sharpstein.
He had a lot better(?) tone, one of these (?) tones, you know. The band altogether sounded like one of the New Orleans band. So you'd give them a lot of march swing, you know.
